messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: empirical.varD
parts:
Good day,

We sample bears at baited hair corrals. We have many trap arrays across our jurisdiction, with 2 - 7 arrays within each of several "Wildlife Zones". Arrays are far enough apart that we treat them as independent (sets of individuals do not intersect).  Arrays all use similar numbers of traps at similar spacing, but vary in shape and extent because we access most trap sites using secondary roads, which are not on a regular grid. Furthermore, some arrays are closer than others to large waterbodies, and we exclude open water as possible locations of activity centers when we define masks, so mask extents vary even more than they would if they were calculated as a simple buffer around traps.

We are interested in estimating average density within Zones, with an appropriate measure of uncertainty, to inform management at this spatial scale. We can easily estimate trapline-specific densities using single-session models, calculate an average density across traplines, and get confidence limits via the delta method. However, we are interested in estimating mean densities directly from the data using multisession models (with CL=T or D~1), with a measure of uncertainty that reflects variation in density among traplines (beyond what would be expected under Poisson or binomial assumptions).

I've been looking at the documentation for empirical.var.D, and it looks like derivedSession() will give us the average density empirical spatial variance we are looking for, without requiring that trap arrays have the same geometry across sessions?

I was wondering if I'm on the right track, and if there's a minimum number of sessions that would be recommended for this approach to be useful, but any advice is welcome!

Eric

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: empirical.varD
parts:
Thanks Murray,
I think see how using fixed-N makes sense (spatially unconditional variance within replicates).

derivedSession() requires a common detection model across sessions (my spatial replicates), however, when I fit models to our multisession data, session effects are sometimes supported; so if I force detection parameters to the same across traplines so that I can use derivedSession, I'd be estimating density from a model that does not fit the data well.

In the distance sampling context, counts of animals (n) on spatial replicates (transects) are weighted by transect length (if it varies).  I was wondering if counts on replicate trap arrays (secr "clusters") could similarly be weighted according to the area sampled. 

For example, they might be scaled by mask area, though this might not work well because buffers and masks are larger than necessary (?).  Nevertheless, given fixed or similar trap spacing across replicates, the mask area provides a relative measure of the area sampled, where differences in mask area among replicates are attributable to differences in geometry, or possibly differences in the amount of non-habitat in the vicinity of traps.

We can also estimate a-hat for each spatial replicate, including from models with session effects, using derived().  These estimates of a-hat capture the differences in the effective sampling area attributable to differences in estimates of detection parameters. However, a-hat ignores differences in the area sampled attributable to differences in cluster geometry (?)

I'm wondering if we could come up with a good way to weight cluster-specific counts by some cluster-specific measure of the area sampled, and also use cluster-specific a-hat to calculate the second component of the variance of Dhat. Perhaps by first calculating mean a-hat across replicates, and var(a-hat) via the delta method?

Any comments welcome.

Eric

parts: This happens to relate to a problem I was working on last month from the viewpoint of study design - how to come up with an unbiased design-based estimate from random or systematic detector clusters across a region when some clusters are truncated by boundary or overlap with non-habitat. With line transects you know the length of transect surveyed so you can make a size-specific adjustment/weighting. With SECR in 2-D there is no well-defined plot 'size'. Using a-hat seems ad hoc but maybe ad hoc is good enough. I have rigged some code and it seems to 'work' in the sense of giving plausible answers, but needs testing. See also attached. Essentially this implements your suggestion. I don't think there's any problem with the second variance component - we're estimating overall D = n/A where A is sum of cluster specific a_i and can sum their variances (assuming independence). Any comments?

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: empirical.varD
parts:
I've been running some trials with various variance estimators, weighted and unweighted. The major results are as expected
- if you have large-scale variation in density across your study area then assuming Poisson n causes the sampling variance (se(D-hat) to be underestimated
- 'empirical' estimates of var(n) by any of the methods (Poisson, weighted or unweighted) are OK (slightly +ve bias of se(D-hat) ) as long as the population is uniformly distributed and clusters are located as a simple random sample
- placing clusters systematically (with random origin) was more efficient than a random sample when density was NOT uniform, but none of the present 'empirical' estimators captured this benefit (i.e. se(D-hat) was overestimated). Weighted was somewhat better than unweighted in this case when cluster size correlates with density - in my example density was high at the coast so high densities were mostly sampled with truncated clusters). The Poisson estimator was very close to true se(D-hat), probably fortuitously.

Systematic designs are definitely recommended, but more work is needed on the variance cf Fewster 2011 Biometrics.

secr 3.2.0 will have the cluster-size-weighted 'empirical' variance options (R2 and R3 of Fewster et al. 2009). But as CRAN incoming is closing for a couple of weeks there will be some delay.

Good day,

I've got some comparative estimates of density with confidence limits from sets of study areas ("traplines") within larger areas of interest (WLZs).
Recall that the spatial configuration of traplines varies, and that we were also concerned about variation in detection parameters among traplines.
Samples from all traplines should be adequate (30 - 60 animals, 3-4 detections per animal on average, plenty of spatial recaptures).
Estimates of sigma are consistent with independent information about sex-specific home range sizes, but variable.






I'd previously completed analyses of trapline-specific data to estimate density in the vicinity of each trapline.
Point estimates of density from different traplines in one WLZ (top figure, 5 traplines) were fairly similar (range 0.00038 - 0.00083 / ha).
Those in the other WLZ were more variable (range 0.00034 - 0.0018 / ha, where the highest estimate was more than double any of the other estimates).

I've since combined traplines within WLZs into multisession capthist objects (traplines as sessions) and conducted analyses to see if detection parameters varied among traplines. They seem to:

Note that for the first (top) WLZ, fitting this model yielded NaN for some variances of g0 or sigma, such that se.esa was not estimable for all traplines, and we could not estimate variances usuing R2.
4): Mean D and CL calculated as above, but from a multisession model that assumes constant g0 and sigma across sessions (despite support for differences; R2; common detectpar).






Conclusions specific to these data:
  1. Ignoring differences in g0 and sigma across traplines within WLZs is not supported, and could bias D-hat, and causes underestimation of the variance of D-hat.

  3. Estimating mean D and associated empirical variance (using R2) directly from trapline-specific results seems reasonable, and avoids the need to fit multisession models.Comments: 

Both D-hat and esa are sensitive to sigma, and therefore to samples of distances moved among traps.  Therefore, when we allow sigma to vary among traplines, D is relatively low and esa is relatively high (independent of array size or configuration) where sigma is relatively high. This means that traplines with high sigma and low D (for similar nj) will generally have higher weight. We can see that estimates of density across traplines are lower than the simple mean of trapline-specific estimates, especially where one of the traplines yielded a much higher density estimate than the others. This seems appropriate (larger area sampled, greater weight), but I might have some concerns about the influence of sigma (is it having too large an effect on the estimates). ????

Murray questioned: Is there a better weighting for the aj in Var(A)?  I wonder - would make a difference if we we avoided squaring linear distances to get areas when weighting? Would that make the weight more similar across traplines of similar configuration?  I.e., reduce the effect of sigma relative to array size in the weights?

Thanks again,
Eric

Good day,

I'm still working up comparisons of varD from replicate sampling units under different assumptions (detection parameters assumed to be constant or variable across replicates, Poisson vs empirical variances).

Two questions about these variance estimators, and their application in 'secr':

(1)  I'm looking at Buckland et al. (2001), Fewster et al. (2009), and, Murray's "replicateclusters.pdf" from 17-12-2018 in this thread.

In "replicateclusters" the first equation for the encounter rate variance for unequal line lengths in DS surveys matches Buckland et al.'s (2001) Equation 3.78 (page 79) for var(n), and the first equation for var(n) from an SECR survey with replicate sampling units is an exact match (substituting a's and A's for l's and L's, respectively).

However, varR2(n) from an SECR survey in replicateclusters.pdf is not an exact match for Fewster et al's (2009) varR2(n/L) from DS surveys (their Equation 3).  In Fewster et al, (k-1) is multiplied by L-squared (total line length squared) in the denominator of the first term, but there is no corresponding multiplication by A-squared (total effective sampling area squared).  Hoping someone can confirm for me that this is the adjustment to estimate var(n) rather than var(n/A) as described in "replicateclusters.pdf"? Thanks very much.

(2) My second question has to do with when replicates should be considered independent, and the 'independent.esa' argument of the derivednj function.  
Our replicates each have ~40 traps, and yielded sufficient data to estimate density in isolation; animals are not detected at > 1 replicate.  I can fit models to "replicate-specific" data, harvest n, a-sub-j, and the SE of a-sub-j from each (using derived), and calculate D and associated measures of uncertainty using derivednj. In this situation, sets of animals are independent, and no information is shared across replicates when estimating detection parameters, so I set indepdendent.esa = T.

I'm also fitting models to multisession data with replicates as sessions (to facilitate comparisons). In this situation, sets of animals do not overlap, but information is shared when estimating the parameters of the detection function, even if I include (additive) session effects. In this situation, since data is shared, should I set independent.esa = F? Thanks again.

Eric

This conversation thread was very helpful. Thanks!

Best,
Manvi

Hi Manvi,

Probably much to late to be useful, sorry I missed this post.
Answer to question 1 is "yes", if any information is shared when estimating parameters
2. I believe this is possible, but may require you to refit models and set contrasts.
3. If meaningful spatial covariates are available, results are likely to be more useful, and more precise. We struggle to identify useful covariates except at large spatial scales, due to lack of spatial resolution in anthropogenic mortality data, and bears' feeding behaviour (seasonal "migration" to abundant food, making it hard to quantify habitat quality within home ranges.)

Eric
